The minimum is

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1+3m^2}{2}, & 0\le m\le \dfrac13,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{4}{27(1-m)^3}, & \dfrac13\le m<1.
\end{cases}}
\]

To prove this, minimize \(\int f^2\) under the two moment constraints. Ignoring \(f\ge 0\), the \(L^2\)-minimizer must lie in the span of \(1,x\), so

\[
f(x)=a+bx.
\]

The constraints give

\[
2a=1,\qquad \frac{2b}{3}=m,
\]

so

\[
f(x)=\frac12+\frac{3m}{2}x.
\]

This is nonnegative on \([-1,1]\) exactly when \(m\le 1/3\). Then

\[
\int_{-1}^1 f^2
=
\int_{-1}^1\left(\frac12+\frac{3m}{2}x\right)^2dx
=
\frac12+\frac{3m^2}{2}.
\]

For \(m>1/3\), the nonnegativity constraint is active. The variational/KKT condition gives an extremizer of the form

\[
f(x)=k(x-c)_+,
\]

supported on \([c,1]\). The constraints determine \(k,c\). First,

\[
1=\int_c^1 k(x-c)\,dx=\frac{k(1-c)^2}{2},
\]

so

\[
k=\frac{2}{(1-c)^2}.
\]

Also,

\[
m=\int_c^1 xk(x-c)\,dx
=
c+\frac{2(1-c)}{3}
=
\frac{2+c}{3}.
\]

Thus

\[
c=3m-2,
\qquad
1-c=3(1-m),
\]

and therefore

\[
\int_{-1}^1 f^2
=
\int_c^1 k^2(x-c)^2\,dx
=
\frac{k^2(1-c)^3}{3}
=
\frac{4}{3(1-c)}
=
\frac{4}{27(1-m)^3}.
\]

At \(m=1/3\), both formulas give \(2/3\), so the piecewise formula matches continuously.
